abstract: This paper investigates whether COVID-19 vaccine misinformation on Facebook had the exposure and persuasive impact required to meaningfully depress US vaccination rates. Combining large-scale survey experiments, crowdsourcing, and machine learning, the authors estimate the causal effect of over 13,000 vaccine-related URLs on the vaccination intentions of roughly 233 million US Facebook users. They find that although fact-check-flagged misinformation was more persuasive per view, its limited reach meant that unflagged but vaccine-skeptical content — much of it from mainstream outlets — had an estimated 46-fold greater overall impact on vaccine hesitancy.
key_claims: Impact on behavior requires two conditions jointly: exposure (people must see content) and persuasive influence (content must change behavior when seen).
Exposure to fact-checked vaccine misinformation can causally reduce vaccination intentions, but its overall societal impact was small because few people saw it.

Unflagged 'vaccine-skeptical' content that is factually accurate but misleading — often from credible mainstream outlets — had a far larger aggregate impact on vaccine hesitancy than flagged misinformation.
The degree to which a story implies vaccines are harmful to health, rather than its veracity, best predicts negative persuasive influence.
Veracity-focused interventions (fact-check labels, domain downranking) target only a small fraction of the content that plausibly caused public health harm.
methods: Two randomized online survey experiments on the Lucid platform (study 1: N = 8,603; study 2: N = 10,122; total N = 18,725) measuring the causal effect of 130 vaccine-related headlines/posts on a pre-post COVID-19 vaccination intentions index.
Study 1 used 40 fact-checker-debunked misinformation items; study 2 used 90 highly shared, quality- and topic-balanced Facebook articles including both true and false content.

Crowd raters labeled the 130 headlines on five dimensions (surprising, plausible, partisan lean, familiar, and harmful-vs-helpful to health); random-effects meta-regressions related these features to treatment effects.
Facebook's Social Science One URL Shares dataset used to measure actual views for 13,206 vaccine-related URLs shared publicly >100 times during January–March 2021, the initial US vaccine rollout.

A crowd-machine pipeline: 177 CloudResearch/MTurk raters predicted persuasive effects to build a 'crowdsourced aggregate score,' which a COVID-Twitter-BERT machine learning model was trained to predict for all 13,206 URLs; predicted scores were passed through the meta-regression to estimate per-URL treatment effects.
Estimated impact computed as the product of per-URL predicted treatment effect and view count, normalized per US Facebook user, with parametric bootstrap confidence intervals and robustness checks.
findings: A single exposure to vaccine misinformation reduced vaccination intentions by 1.5 percentage points on average (P = 0.00004), with effects varying by item (bottom decile ~3 pp reduction; top decile ~0).

Only the 'harmful-to-health' dimension consistently predicted negative persuasive effect; a 1-point increase corresponded to about −0.69 pp; veracity was non-significant once harm-to-health was controlled.
Flagged misinformation URLs received only 8.7 million views — 0.3% of the 2.7 billion vaccine-related URL views; low-credibility domains accounted for 5.1% of views.

A single unflagged Chicago Tribune article ('A healthy doctor died two weeks after getting a COVID vaccine') was seen by ~54.9 million people (>20% of US Facebook users), and its story cluster received over six times the views of all flagged misinformation combined.

The crowdsourced aggregate score predicted observed treatment effects well (sampling-error-adjusted correlation 0.75, P = 0.0001, pseudo-R² = 0.34); the BERT model achieved 97% AUC and 91% accuracy on a hesitancy-inducing binary task.
The median flagged URL had a predicted effect of −1.36 pp versus −0.30 pp for the median unflagged URL, but weighting by views reversed the overall picture.

Vaccine-skeptical (unflagged, hesitancy-inducing) content lowered vaccination intentions by an estimated −2.28 pp per US Facebook user versus −0.05 pp for flagged misinformation — a 46-fold difference; 98% of views of hesitancy-inducing content were unflagged.
Low-credibility domains accounted for only 9.3% of the total estimated decrease; mainstream outlets (e.g., New York Post, Fox News, local news) drove the largest overall negative impact.
Aggregate impact translates to roughly 2.3 pp lower intentions per user, corresponding to an estimated ~3 million fewer vaccinated Americans (assuming behavior effects are 60% of intention effects).
contributions: Introduces a scalable framework that decomposes societal impact into exposure × persuasive influence and operationalizes it with experiments, crowdsourcing, and NLP.
Provides one of the first causal-scale estimates of misinformation's real-world impact rather than relying on correlational or proxy measures.
Demonstrates a crowd-plus-machine-learning pipeline that generalizes experimental treatment effects to thousands of real-world URLs using minimal platform data.
Reframes the misinformation debate to emphasize factually accurate but misleading 'gray-area' content, especially from mainstream sources.
Offers policy-relevant tools for continuously identifying high-impact harmful content that veracity-based moderation misses, applicable to other outcomes and platforms.
framing: The paper situates itself within misinformation and computational social science research, challenging the prevailing 'infodemic' assumption that viral falsehoods drove vaccine refusal. It positions itself against a large correlational literature and prior lab studies by explicitly separating veracity from persuasive impact and by measuring exposure and behavioral intentions at ecosystem scale, extending the bottom-up, integrative approach to studying platform effects on society.
